Package Structure

structure.Rmd

This vignette describes how nomad links fitted models to information about their source data, and what happens when we use a model to make a prediction. It may be useful if you want to understand the package objects or contribute a model of your own.

Core Objects

The central object is a nomad_model, which contains a mobility::mobility() model together with its source metadata and saved fit checks. It is an R6 object, so its methods can be called with $, for example model$get_model() to retrieve the underlying mobility model. Functions such as predict(model) and summary(model) provide the usual R interface to common operations.

The package data objects are:

  1. model_db: a named list of fitted nomad_model objects.
  2. mobility_db: a table describing the source mobility datasets.

The link between them is the source data name. For example, zmb_fb_2020_mod_grav_exp is a model fit to the zmb_fb_2020 mobility dataset.

User Workflow

A typical analysis has five steps:

  1. Search mobility_table() and model_table() for relevant source data and fitted models.
  2. Inspect the source scale with model_profile().
  3. Prepare prediction data: a distance matrix and population vector.
  4. Predict a mobility matrix with predict().
  5. Inspect warnings and compare predictions or ensembles to see how model choice affects the analysis.

Population helpers such as get_pop() and unpack_pop() support the data preparation step, but users can also supply their own population vectors and distance matrices directly.

From stored fit to prediction

The model database contains 612 Facebook fits across 51 country or territory datasets, together with the two original Zambia fits. Several model families can be fit to the same dataset, which is why there are many more models than source datasets. The has_fitted_models column in mobility_db is calculated from this link and tells us whether an entry has models available for use. This also allows a dataset to be described in the catalogue before its models have been contributed to the model database.

For the newer Facebook datasets, the observed trip matrices are private and are removed before the models are packaged. The distances and population sizes are stored separately in inst/extdata/model_data, with one copy per dataset shared by its fitted models. Calling get_model() restores these covariates when they are needed for a prediction. We also retain the supplied fit statistics and diagnostic plots, allowing users to inspect the source fit without access to the underlying trip observations.

Both predict(model) and model$predict() use the same prediction method. Before calling mobility, this method checks that the supplied distances and populations refer to the same regions, matches named inputs to their required order, and converts distances from the user’s declared units to those used for fitting. It also checks whether the model supports prediction for the requested setting. These checks are useful when comparing several models, since their original datasets may use different units or contain different sets of regions.

Most model families can predict for new populations and distances using their fitted parameters. Basic and finite radiation models instead retain a prediction matrix tied to their original regions and populations. nomad checks this restriction before asking mobility for a prediction, including when the model is part of an ensemble. This prevents a stored matrix from being returned as though it described a different set of regions. A new radiation prediction needs to be calculated from the inputs for that new setting.

Duration conversion takes place using the prediction period in the model metadata. This period describes the interval represented by the predicted counts and can differ from the dates over which observations were collected. For example, a matrix averaged across several weekly observations would still need a period for the counts in each matrix, rather than the length of the whole collection window. Allowing an unknown period in the metadata means that a contributed model can still be included before all its source information is available. Its unscaled predictions can be explored with a warning, while operations that require the missing information, such as conversion to a chosen number of days, raise an error. Completing the metadata makes the same model useful for a wider range of analyses.

An ensemble calls the prediction method for each component before combining the results. The output matrices are matched by their target-region names, so the models can have been fit in different places as long as they can predict for the same requested regions. Their prediction periods must also agree, or be convertible to a common duration. Finally, named weights are matched to their models and used to average the aligned trip counts. Matching by name makes this independent of the order in which models happen to appear in a table.
